source.title: Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Next Location Predictors
source.authors: Ciro Beneduce; Bruno Lepri; Massimiliano Luca

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and supplementary information are present.
record.tranche_reason: It compares downstream next-location accuracy across LLMs of different stated sizes, using accuracy rather than held-out cross-entropy or fitted scaling laws. This bears on V6, but it does not reproduce the original scaling-law measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates next-location accuracy, not held-out pretraining loss, power-law fits, extrapolation from small runs, or compute-optimal allocations. The LLM size and accuracy results in Table SI 47 are recorded for V6. Other results, including prompt and historical/context ablations, are not separate rows here because they do not test whether downstream performance scales predictably with model size or pretraining loss. The paper cites Kaplan et al.; cited findings are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: In a new downstream task (zero-shot next-location prediction, ACC@5), the study compares models of different parameter counts within the Llama 2, Llama 3 and Llama 3 Instruct families. The authors state that bigger models perform better, citing Kaplan et al. This is a directional, few-point size comparison in a new setting, so T3 fits better than T2. There is no fitted law and no use of pretraining loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct, but secondary. The main conclusion is that LLMs work as zero-shot next-location predictors, reaching up to 0.362 ACC@5 and far exceeding transferred DL baselines. On size, the authors say bigger models perform better (citing Kaplan et al.), note exceptions such as Mistral 7B beating Llama 2 13B, and say smaller Llama models struggle with few-shot prompts. They fit no law.
record.recipe_differences: Uses zero-, one-, and few-shot next-location evaluation with ACC@5 on mobility datasets, rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy sweeps or power-law fitting.
record.method_sensitivity: Prompt strategy changes reported accuracy; the paper also reports that dataset and availability of historical/contextual visits affect accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report that the detail of the explanations the models give for their predictions depends mainly on parameter count: larger models cite specific location IDs. This is a qualitative observation with no metric.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger LLMs produce more specific rationales for their predictions.

record.problems: The downstream comparison is not a controlled scaling sweep: model families and training stages differ, parameter counts are not stated for GPT models, and the paper does not fit a size-accuracy curve or test predictive extrapolation. Table SI 47 gives no uncertainty values for its prompt/model accuracies, although the text says results and standard deviations were obtained from three independent runs.
record.rows_left_out: Table SI 47 also reports Tokyo and Ferrara ACC@5 for the same 15 models and three prompt strategies. Those 90 rows were left out to stay within the 60-row limit; the paper says trends and conclusions are similar across cities. Other task/context ablations and ACC@1/ACC@3 results were not included because they do not add direct tests of size-related downstream predictability.

untested.parts: No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No power-law form in other modalities or regimes.
No relation to pretraining loss. No fitted or quantitatively predicted size–accuracy curve; at most three sizes per family. Single task.

missing.what: Eight smaller or older models (Phi-1.5, Phi-2, Phi-3, Gemma 2B, GPT-J, Dolly 3B/7B/12B) failed the task with empty or unusable outputs. This is a size- and capability-related downstream result not recorded or declared in rows_left_out.
missing.locator: Introduction; Methods 'Large Language Models'; Supplementary Information 3 'Failed Models'

missing.what: Within-family size trends are replicated for Tokyo and Ferrara. For example, Llama 2 Chat one-shot 7B (0.178) again beats 13B (0.162) in Tokyo. These cities are declared as left out, but they confirm the prompt-dependent break.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3: this is an application in a new setting with an incidental size comparison, not a method aimed at scaling. The evidence is weak for V6's 'predictably': two or three sizes per family, no loss and no fit. Model families confound data and recipe. Table SI 47's default-configuration values lack SDs; SDs of about 0.01 appear in Table SI 49 for the ablations, small relative to most within-family gaps but comparable to some (e.g. the 7B vs 13B chat one-shot gap of 0.017).

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No power-law fits on small runs or predictions of larger runs.
No fixed-compute comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
No scaling-law tests across modalities or training regimes.
Measures ACC@5 on one downstream task, not a fitted relationship or predictions from pretraining loss; it does not establish predictability on other downstream tasks.
No fitted exponents, compute-optimal split, or comparison of scaling-law fitting choices.

relationships.condition: Within-family comparisons: Llama 2 base (all prompts), Llama 3 base and Llama 3 Instruct (all prompts), Llama 2 Chat zero-shot; Foursquare NYC ACC@5
relationships.reason: ACC@5 rises monotonically with parameter count in each of these series (e.g. Llama 2 base 0.077/0.105/0.163; Llama 3 Instruct 0.165→0.338). This is directional only, not a fitted prediction.
relationships.display_finding: ACC@5 increased monotonically within each specified series, including Llama 2 base from 0.077 to 0.105 to 0.163 and Llama 3 Instruct from 0.165 to 0.338.

relationships.condition: Llama 2 Chat with one-shot and few-shot prompts
relationships.reason: The size order breaks: 7B beats 13B under one-shot (0.185 vs 0.168) and few-shot (0.066 vs 0.047), so the trend depends on the prompt choice (r02, r03, r05, r06, r08, r09).
relationships.display_finding: The 7B model beat 13B with one-shot prompting, 0.185 versus 0.168, and few-shot prompting, 0.066 versus 0.047.

relationships.reason: Parameter count alone does not order performance. Mistral 7B (0.156) beats Llama 2 13B (0.105), as the authors note. Llama 3 8B Instruct (0.165) beats Llama 3 70B base (0.148), so the training stage matters more than size (r43, r13, r34, r31).
relationships.display_finding: Mistral 7B scored 0.156 versus 0.105 for Llama 2 13B, while Llama 3 8B Instruct scored 0.165 versus 0.148 for Llama 3 70B base.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Across the tested LLMs in the paper's general comparison of model sizes
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that larger models generally perform better, and the New York zero-shot results include higher ACC@5 for larger members of several same-family comparisons, including Llama 2 base and Llama 3 base/instruct models (r10, r13, r16, r28, r31, r34, r37). This is a directional result, not a fitted prediction law.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Across model families and prompting strategies on Foursquare New York
reader_labels.reason: Performance is not determined by parameter count alone: the paper notes Mistral 7B outperforms Llama 2 13B, and the reported ACC@5 varies substantially with prompting for some models, including Llama 2 13B Chat (r04-r06) and Llama 3 70B Instruct (r37-r39).
